study.title: 2 Corinthians 10 - Defense of Paul's ministry and the real motive for approval
study.overview: In this chapter, Paul responds to the accusation of weakness and self-exalting by opponents in Corinth. He asks that the church not judge him by appearance or human standards, but to recognize that his authority comes from the Lord to build, not destroy. The chapter contrasts religious pride with true approval: it is not approved who praises itself, but who is praised by the Lord. The section also shows that Paul's struggle is not carnal; his weapons are spiritual and effective to overthrow ideas and superb contrary to the knowledge of God.

outline.title: Paul appeals with meekness and responds to the accusation
outline.explanation: He presents himself with humility and asks that he will not be forced to act hard when he is present. The criticism that he acts according to the flesh is rejected, because his posture is not motivated by human interests.

outline.title: Spiritual battle and apostolic discipline
outline.explanation: Paul states that, although he lives in a human body, he does not fight with fleshly methods. The weapons given by God overthrow mental and proud fortifications, leading thoughts to the obedience of Christ. The authority received also includes correcting disobedience when the obedience of the church is mature.

outline.title: Wrong Criterion, True Authority and Measure from God
outline.explanation: Paul fights judgment for appearance and vain self-comparedness. He shows that his authority was given to build the church and that he is not invading the work of others. His hope is to be even more useful when the faith of the Corinthians grows, to proclaim the gospel elsewhere without being proud of what was done by another.

outline.title: Glory must be in the Lord
outline.explanation: The abstract of the argument is that true praise is not his own, but what comes from the Lord. The decisive approval does not come from self-praise, but from the assessment of God.

study.context: The chapter is linked to the defense of Paul's ministry in front of opponents in Corinth. The notes highlight a change of tone in relation to the previous chapters: now Paul is on the defensive, responding to accusations and preserving the church from false influences. The sources also observe that there were rival teachers in Corinth, and that Paul was attacked for appearing weak in presence, although he was firm in letters.
study.theology: The text teaches that Christian authority is neither personal dominion nor display of strength, but service received from God for the edification of the people. The gospel struggle is spiritual, for ideas, prides and human claims must be confronted by the truth of Christ. There is also a direct criticism of religious pride: comparing oneself with oneself, seeking self-promotion and measuring success by appearance are misleading ways. Approval before God is linked to faithful service, praise to the Lord and to the obedience of Christ, not to self-promotion. In evangelical reading, this preserves the centrality of Christ and grace, even though discipline and firmness are also part of the legitimate ministry.

scholarViews.insight: Paul reacts to criticism by showing that his authority is given to build the people of God, not to destroy them, and that he will deal firmly with rivals when necessary.
Paul speaks with meekness and humility, taking the meekness of Christ as a model in defending his ministry without wanting to provoke unnecessary hardship.
The accusation that Paul would be strong only by letters and weak in presence is rejected as judgment according to appearance, a deceptive criterion.

questions: In what situations do I usually judge people or ministries by appearance, not by spiritual fruit?
Do my words and attitudes seek to build others in Christ or just protect my image?
What, in practice, today means boasting in the Lord and not in myself?
study.practice: This week, evaluate an opinion you've formed about someone in the church and ask if it was based on appearance, comparison, or real fruit. Pray before speaking, seeking to act meekly, but without abandoning the truth. Instead of seeking personal recognition, make a concrete act of anonymous service and thank God for whatever good He produces through you.
study.uncertainty: The text provided is the main basis, and the notes allow to safely affirm the contrast between meekness, spiritual authority, criticism of self-comparison and praise in the Lord. However, details of the exact identity of the opponents, the precise historical composition of the section and the extent of the Jeremiah 9:24 quotation cannot be treated as certain only with the given notes. There is also variation between commentators on aspects of the chapter structure and apostolic measure in 10:13-16.
